title: Marianne Cope (1838–1918)
hookLine: a German-American sister who went to nurse in Hawaii and, the accounts of her life say, stayed thirty years at Molokai

cards: Hungry for the work. Those are the words a convent superior in Syracuse, New York, writes back to Hawaii. A priest there is looking for sisters to nurse people with leprosy.
He has asked community after community, and they have said no. She has a hospital to run in New York, sisters who rely on her, a life full of work already.
Still, she answers that she wants to go, and that she wishes with all her heart to be one of the chosen ones.

teach.h: AN IMMIGRANT GIRL IN A FACTORY.
teach.b: Her name was Marianne Cope, a Franciscan sister. The Church now calls her Saint Marianne of Molokai. First, the immigrant girl.
She was born in Germany, and her family came to New York state when she was small. As a young woman she worked in a factory to help support them, and only later could she enter religious life.

In Syracuse and Utica her community opened hospitals, and she helped run them. They took in patients other hospitals turned away. She learned how to organize care, keep a ward clean, and stand up for the sick.
Third, Hawaii. She sailed with a small group of sisters, nursed first in Honolulu, and then went to Kalaupapa on Molokai.

teach.h: SHE NURSES DAMIEN AT THE END.
teach.b: She arrived as Father Damien was dying. She nursed him, and after his death she took over the care of the boys he had looked after.
She ran a new home for women and girls, and insisted on cleanliness, on gardens, on pretty things like flowers and ribbons, so that a place of exile could feel like a home.
Fourth, the staying. The accounts of her life say she stayed thirty years at Molokai, and she died there. She did not go back to New York.

Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Bear ye one another's burdens; and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ." Damien carried the people of Kalaupapa. Marianne carried Damien, and then his work.

how: Catholics in Hawaii and in Syracuse, New York, keep Saint Marianne Cope's feast on January 23, and Catholic hospitals and nurses often remember her as an example of care for the sick.

games.q: you run a hospital in New York. a letter arrives asking for sisters to nurse people with leprosy in Hawaii. others have said no. what do you do?
o: say no; your hospital needs you.
games.why: she wrote back that she was hungry for the work, and went herself with a small group of sisters.

practice: Think of someone who looks after others: a nurse, a parent with a newborn, someone caring for an aging mother, the friend who always shows up. Picture their tired face at the end of the day, and ask who looks after them.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, hold them in mind with gratitude.
